utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-01-47-T, Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper. And for the duration of the examination of the military expert our legal intern, Mr. Kyle Wood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. JUDGE ANTONETTI: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could a correction be made. The legal assistant for the Defence is Muriel Cauvin not Mirna Milanovic, which is what it says in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's quite right. The correction will be made. After the long weekend, the Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, and in particular, the Prosecution's assistant who is responsible for military affairs. I would also like to greet Defence counsel, the accused, and all those present in this courtroom, the two new interns, and the interpreters, as well as the security officers. We have an expert witness scheduled for today. He will be testifying over a period of several days. Before we call this expert witness into the courtroom, the Trial Chamber would like to inform the Defence counsel that the Judges, who will have questions, think that this will take at least one hearing. It will certainly be Friday, or perhaps Thursday, if the cross-examination doesn't take as long as expected. So I'd like to encourage the Defence to not use up more time than is allocated to them. Otherwise, the Judges won't have time to ask their questions. If the schedule is adhered to, we'll be able to conclude at the end of the week and the documents that still have to be dealt with, Mr. Bourgon still has four or five documents to deal with, they can be dealt with and Mr. Dixon also has to express his position with regard to the categories of documents he has mentioned. If we can finish with this stage this week it will enable the Trial Chamber to render its decision concerning the documents. Without wasting any more time, I will now ask the usher to call the witness, unless Mr. Dixon has something he would like to say perhaps. He won't be addressing the issue of categories after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's just one matter I wish to raise on behalf of both Defence counsel and that follows on from what Your Honour has mentioned about the methodology of examining the expert witness. It is our understanding, and I've spoken to my learned friend from the Prosecution about this, that no documents will in fact be tendered through this witness when he gives his evidence in chief. He will have the documents available for him to refer to, but there will be no application to tender any of those documents into evidence. I am advised by my learned friends that the examination-in-chief will be very brief, probably no longer than about an hour and a half to two hours. Your Honours will recall I did raise some concern about this matter a while ago, and Your Honours were absolutely correct. It's not for Defence to indicate how the Prosecution should examine in chief. However, there is one matter that we would seek Your Honours' guidance on and that is that the re-examination of the witness after we've cross-examined should not become an examination-in-chief. If the Prosecution elects now to keep it very brief and the Defence then cross-examines, the usual rules should apply, that they can only re-examine on those matters that are raised by the Defence, and in particular, only refer to documents that are either referred to by the General in his examination-in-chief or that the Defence raises in cross-examination. But not reintroduce a whole range of new documents right at the end, when the Defence won't have an opportunity to cross-examine thereafter. I think that is acceptable to my learned friends, having spoken to them earlier, but we were just somewhat concerned that if the examination-in-chief was very brief, that the opportunities shouldn't then be taken at the end to open up many new issues when the cross-examination would have been completed already. Your Honour, that's the only matter we wish to raise about the method in which the examination will take place. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just a minute, Mr. Mundis. I will let you take the floor in a minute to respond. The Trial Chamber usually summarises what has been said, for the following reason: As the proceedings are relayed to the outside, those following the proceedings might not be in a position to understand the meaning of something that is being said, given that what is being said might refer to previous hearings and the person following the proceedings on the outside might be perplexed and uncertain of what is happening. So for pedagogical reasons, the Trial Chamber has been attempting to summarise in general terms what is being said, and it's true that the Defence, generally speaking, has already raised this issue. They did so a few days ago. The issue is the following one: The Prosecution told us that it reserved the right to have one and a half hours or two hours to conduct its examination-in-chief. And the Defence told us that they would need a number of days to cross-examine the witness. This was accepted by the Trial Chamber. Given that these days should take up about 50 per cent more than the time taken by the Prosecution. If the Prosecution takes two hours, then the Defence would only have the right to have three hours. But given the importance of the testimony that we will be hearing, it would be appropriate for the Defence to be in a position to ask all questions that are useful within the framework of these adversarial proceedings. That is why we have planned to question the witness for a few days. But the Defence was concerned about the issue of the Prosecution re-examining the witness, and the Defence has mentioned two problems in relation to this matter. When re-examining the witness, will the Prosecution be tendering documents into evidence, and within the framework of their re-examination, will the Prosecution be dealing with issues that weren't raised in the course of the examination-in-chief? In theory, additional questions, by definition, are questions that have to do with the cross-examination, because if the examination-in-chief has been properly conducted, there is no need for additional questions. Because all this has been addressed or should have been addressed in the course of the examination-in-chief. If there are any other additional questions, it means that after the cross-examination, there are new issues, new questions, which make it necessary for the Prosecution to ask the witness more questions. It is within this framework that additional questions are asked. This was the position expressed by the Defence, a position we have just summarised with regard to additional questions. Can the Prosecution now inform us of its position as far as their view of additional questions are concerned. Mr. Mundis, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Let me briefly respond to the comments of my learned colleague Mr. Dixon. Mr. President, the Prosecution has at this time no intention of conducting a lengthy re-examination of the witness. Again, as long as we remain within the general confines of examination and cross-examination, then certainly the re-examination would follow only from those areas of cross-examination that the Prosecution might feel a need to clear up for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. Of course, with an expert witness, it's a slightly different scenario in that the expert has filed and provided to Your Honours an expert report or statement. The Prosecution, as I will explain in just a moment, will not be necessarily leading or adducing evidence as to each and every paragraph contained in that statement, but will primarily for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and the public at large, adduce evidence from this expert report in a bullet-type format, if you will, to explain the salient portions of that report for the benefit of Your Honours and the public. Of course, at the end of the examination-in-chief of the witness, the Prosecution will tender into evidence the full expert report, and of course the Defence will be entitled to cross-examine, not only on the oral testimony of the expert but upon his methodology and in fact on all of the conclusions he reaches in his report. If I may, Your Honour, I would like to explain very briefly, because I'm quite aware of the tick tock of the clock, how the Prosecution is planning on proceeding this afternoon. I do not anticipate that the direct examination will take longer than 90 minutes, and in fact I will be endeavouring to complete the examination at or about the time of our first break. For obvious reasons, the expert will have -- or we would propose that he be allowed to have his expert statement in front of him as he testifies. We also would ask the Trial Chamber to allow the expert to have those documents which he has referred to in his footnotes in front of him and accessible to him. The witness will testify as to the extremely large amount of material that he was provided with in order to compile his report. General Reinhardt has in fact collated that material and currently has all of the documents to which he cites in his footnotes assembled into two arch-lever binders which he has then tabbed by footnote number. The Prosecution would submit, Your Honours, that it would be a means of saving vast amounts of time for him to have before him, or accessible to him, those two binders with the documents he has cited to, so that he can quickly refer back to the documents in order to answer any questions put to him by any of the parties or by Your Honours. While it is true, as Mr. Dixon has said, the Prosecution will not tender documents through the witness, it is equally true that the Prosecution in its direct examination does not intend on asking or showing the expert witness specific documents. However, we anticipate in responding to questions, such as: How, sir, did you reach that conclusion? That the expert will have recourse to the documents that he cites to and should then be given the opportunity, if need be, to flip to those documents in order to highlight a point or to read out a particular passage that supports the conclusions he reached in his report. So again, Mr. President, with the leave of the Chamber, we would propose that the expert have available to him at the witness bench both his statement, or expert report, and the binders that he has with him containing the documents which he cites to in the footnotes of that report. The Prosecution will then take the expert relatively briefly through the various conclusions that he has reached along the lines of the subject headings that are stated in his report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. You focused on the methodology, but you haven't answered the question that concerns Mr. Dixon, and that is the issue of additional questions. What is your position with regard to additional questions? What you have just said, does that mean that there won't be any additional questions unless new elements arise in the course of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As Your Honours might appreciate, it's a bit difficult to answer that question in anything other than very general terms. In the event that the Defence remains within the four corners, if you will, of the expert's report, it's not anticipated that we would have a lengthy redirect examination. However, if the Defence were to take a different approach whereby they would use this expert to testify about a large number of issues that are not contained in his report or perhaps to show him a relatively large number of documents which the Prosecution is not aware of or has not seen, then that would be a completely different story. I will, Mr. President, assure Your Honours and the Defence that it is not our intention in conducting a relatively short direct examination to then use redirect as a means of then adducing several hours of additional testimony for which the Defence would not be perhaps given an opportunity to fully cross-examine the witness. We certainly have no intention of doing that, Mr. President. But again, as Your Honours will appreciate, it's difficult for me to say how long I will take on redirect until the cross-examination is over and we see precisely what areas outside of the expert report the expert has been asked to comment upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. You've been very clear. So we can draw the following conclusions from what you say. There are two issues you addressed. Firstly, the issue of the methodology. As far as this witness is concerned, this witness should have his statement with him and the two binders. Since both the Defence and the Trial Chamber had these, there are footnotes in the statement and as the statement is based on documents, it's necessary for the witness to be able to refer to the documents. So this would make it possible to save a lot of time, because the witness will immediately be able to locate the document that is being discussed at a given point in time. And as a result, it won't be necessary for the Prosecution or the Defence to find the document and show it to the witness. This seems to be the best and most appropriate methodology to follow. As far as Mr. Dixon's concerns are concerned, it seems that you have answered this question. Mr. Dixon, you said that the point of main interest is the statement, just the statement. And additional questions would only be raised if the Defence addresses new issues or refers to new documents. If issues are addressed -- new issues are addressed, issues that aren't contained in the report, then the Prosecution will ask additional questions, and if necessary, they will ask these questions on the basis of the cross-examination. This is what the Prosecution stated. Mr. Dixon, is there anything else you would like to say about the clarifications that Mr. Mundis has provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. At this stage, not. The main point was to, as Your Honours indicated, to confine the re-examination only to questions that are raised by the Defence that could not have been dealt with in the examination-in-chief on the basis of the statement and the documents that are before General Reinhardt. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Madam Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Reinhardt, I would first like to check that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying. If you're receiving the English interpretation, because we don't have any German interpretation, please tell me that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the case, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have been called to testify here as an expert witness for the Prosecution, and as a witness for the Prosecution, you should take the solemn declaration. Before you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. do so, you should tell me your first and last names and your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my name is Klaus Reinhardt. I was born on the 15th of January, 1941 in Berlin Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What position do you hold at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just a husband of my wife. I have no additional position right now, sir. I'm a retired general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In 1993, ten years ago, what duties did you perform, from January to December 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1993 I was still the commandant of the Commander General Staff College in Hamburg Germany 1993, and then I transferred to Koblenz to become the commanding general of the 3rd German Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified before an International Court or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I never testified in international or national court. This is my first experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read the declaration you have in your hands, the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. As I have already said, you have been called here as an expert witness for the Prosecution. Before the Prosecution takes the floor, I would like to provide you with some information regarding the procedure that will be followed here during this hearing and the following hearings. I think that the parties have already provided you with such information. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber would like to inform you of how this hearing will proceed. In particular, because of the media. You have just taken the solemn declaration, which naturally means that your testimony should be precise. You shouldn't give false testimony, because when a witness gives false testimony, such a witness could be prosecuted. But this is a purely academic issue, given your position. There is another provision, but that doesn't apply to you. This provision concerns a witness who refuses to answer a question because his answer might incriminate him. In such a case, the witness doesn't have to reply to the question, but the Trial Chamber can compel the witness to answer the question, though the witness would be granted a form of immunity. But as an expert witness, this is not something that would usually be applicable to you. In the course of these proceedings, which are of an Anglo-Saxon kind, you will have to answer the Prosecution's questions. They will conduct their examination-in-chief. You have already met the members of the Prosecution, and they will ask you questions on the basis of the written report that you drafted at their request. The Prosecution has told us that their examination-in-chief should take between an hour and a half and two hours, at the most. Once the Prosecution has concluded its examination-in-chief -- you will have your written statement before you, and you will also have two binders containing the various documents that you need in order to answer questions. Once this stage has been concluded, Defence counsel, and they are to your left, there are six of them, but only two of them will be asking you questions within the framework of their cross-examination. The purpose of the cross-examination is to verify the witness's credibility and the Defence can also ask the witness any questions that they might think are useful, questions that concern military issues, technical issues, the relevant period, et cetera. So this is the cross-examination, which will take a number of days, given the length and importance of your report. And the Defence has requested a number of days for the conduct of their cross-examination. Once they have concluded their cross-examination, the Prosecution may ask you additional questions which will arise from the answers you have given to the questions put to you by Defence counsel. So that will be the re-examination. And on the last day, perhaps on Friday, the three Judges, who are sitting before you, will also ask you some questions. The purpose of these questions will be to clarify the answers you have provided to the parties. All these questions will be questions that the Judges want to ask you in order to clarify important issues that are not clear or that haven't been mentioned. After the Judges have asked their questions, the Prosecution and Defence may take the floor again so that you can complete the answers you had given the Judges. As an expert witness, and this is something that you have surely understood, there will be a debate that concerns your expert report. Generally speaking, this is how the proceedings will unfold. Try to provide complete and precise answers to the questions put to you, because the procedure followed here is an oral procedure. Everything is done orally and it is on this basis that the Judges need to be informed. That's why your answers are important. If a question doesn't seem clear to you, ask the person asking you the question to rephrase it. In addition, in the course of the cross-examination, you will have to answer very precise questions put to you by the Defence. The Trial Chamber will ensure that the questions are put to you simply and clearly to ensure that the Trial Chamber understands your answers. Very often, the answer we expect you to give will be yes or no, but the Trial Chamber will ensure that your answers are intelligible and clear for the Judges, because the Judges have to come to their conclusions on the basis of your answers. If you encounter any difficulties in the course of this hearing or in the course of future hearings, inform the Trial Chamber of this. We are here to deal with any difficulties. We are at your disposal and we can help you in the course of this week. We have a little time before the break. The hearing goes on for one and a half hours and then we have half an hour break for technical reasons. It's not because the Trial Chamber needs to rest. We need to have a break after an hour and a half so that the technicians can change the tape. We could all go on for a number of hours, but for technical reasons, we have to have this technical break after an hour and a half. Mr. Mundis, I think you will be conducting the examination-in-chief. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Reinhardt.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you please describe for them your military career, beginning from the time you joined the German army.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I joined the German army in October 1960, as a recruit in a military infantry unit, and I stayed there for the next two years to become an officer's candidate. And after I finished my training as an officer, I was a platoon commander for five years in the same battalion, became the operations officer of that battalion before I went to the University of Freiburg to study history and political science. After I finished my studies, I became a company commander in the neighbouring mountain infantry battalion, before I went to the Command and General Staff College in Hamburg to get my general staff training which was followed by the General Staff training of the US army Command and General Staff College in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. From there I had my first NATO assignment as a planner in headquarter CENTAG in Heidelberg, from which I was called to act as the military assistant of the vice chief of the German armed forces. I then became a battalion commander of a mountain infantry battalion for two years. From there I went to the headquarters of the 1st Mountain Division in Garmisch-Partenkirchen as the operations officer, and half a year as a Chief of Staff before I became the military assistant of the then minister of defence, Manfred Worner. Afterwards, I went back to the mountain troops as the commander of the one and only mountain infantry brigade in Bad Reichenhall, from where I went back to Bonn as the chief planner of the German armed forces. In this capacity, I had to unite the east and west German military forces. I then became the commandant of the Command and General Staff College in Hamburg, then went to Koblenz as the commanding general of the 3rd Corps, which I had to disband and build up a new organisation which we call the German army forces command, which was built up for deployment out of area. So I commanded in this capacity our troops, our national troops in Somalia, in UNPROFOR, in IFOR and SFOR. Under the UN and then NATO command, I then became the commander of the commanding general of the headquarter LANDCENT in Heidelberg, and in this capacity I deployed with my staff as KFOR staff to Kosovo for six months. And then in the last year of my career, I came back in the key mission as the commander of this headquarters was to get the Polish and the Czech land forces into NATO, and I retired from the military in April, end of March 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I have a few follow-on questions from your CV, if you will, that you've just explained to us. First, you mentioned that you finished your studies in history and political science. What degree, what was the highest degree you earned in terms of your formal academic studies?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I wrote the thesis and on this -- for this thesis and the examinations I got the Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, you also mentioned - and I know this is common for career military officers such as yourself - a few acronyms or abbreviations. For the benefit of the Chamber, I just wanted to ask you about a couple of those. You mentioned CENTAG. That's C-E-N-T-A-G. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what CENTAG is?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. CENTAG is the central army group. This is the land component of the NATO forces from the Nordkapp to the Alps, responsible for all the forces stationed and organised in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, you also mentioned LANDCENT. Can you tell us what LANDCENT refers to.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is almost identical to what I just said. It is -- it was a new name giving for almost the same thing, with the exception that we had very strong navy, naval and air components within this headquarters. But basically again it embraced the entire area from the Nordkapp to the Alps, as far as army forces were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General, based on what you've told us, would it be fair to conclude that during your 40-year military career, you held a number of command positions from platoon commander all the way through and including corps commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm very proud that most of the time in my career I was a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, do you recall approximately when you were first contacted by the Office of the Prosecutor with respect to this case?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: It's almost two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what your tasking was, or what the Office of the Prosecutor asked you to do?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, I was asked whether I would look through a variety of documents in order to try to check on the status of the Mujahedin and the chain of command in the Bosnian armed forces as far as the 7th Mountain Infantry Brigade, and in particular, the Mujahedin, were concerned. And at the beginning, I was just given that material. I had to scan it, and I should answer to the questions I have been provided for by the Prosecution whether I could get a special -- closer feeling on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I should just caution you that because we are speaking the same language, we need to pause between question and answer so that the interpreters can keep up with us. So if I briefly pause, I would ask you to periodically do the same. General, that initial contact that you had with the Office of the Prosecutor, did that subsequently expand? That is, were you subsequently given a larger task to perform?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I was called back here and we had our first discussion, and it was still open whether I would take the task to look through the material in more detail and be the witness, and I thought it was a very interesting case, so I said yes, and I got additional material, I got additional questions I had to answer, and this was an interrelation which was established from thereon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, can you tell the Trial Chamber approximately how much material and what type of material the Office of the Prosecutor provided you with?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, I'll be very frankly [sic], when I got the material for the first time I was rather shocked because I got two moving [sic] full of material, and in the meantime, I got additional material, including my own excerpts -- it's almost 23 binders, thick and smaller binders of material, documents, witness statements, orders, excerpts of war diaries, this kind of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber the methodology that you used with respect to the 23 binders of material that you received? What did you do with it? How did you approach this material?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I have been given answers [sic] by the Prosecution which I was asked to answer, based on those documents. So I scanned at the beginning to get a basic overview of the whole material, and then I matched the questions I've been given to the documents. I went through. I had a matrix of those questions and basically had to find through these documents the appropriate documents which could answer, in a positive or negative way, the answers I was asked to work on. So this was a very time-consuming and tedious way, and I had to go through this at least two times, because additional questions were coming up and then I had to start the whole thing again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I have a question of clarification. At page 19, line 3 in the transcript, which you might see before you on the screen, you indicate -- you said: I have been given answers by the Prosecution which I was asked to answer. Were you in fact given answers by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No. Sorry. Sorry. Excuse me for my pigeon English. I was given questions I had to answer. No, I was never given answers, and I was never somehow told whether my answers were appropriate or not. I was just given questions, and I tried to answer them the best way as possible, based on the abundancy of material provided to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, do the subtopics, if you will -- your report sets forth a number of subtopics. Do those generally relate to the questions that the Prosecution asked you to focus on?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that among the material that you received were witness statements. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what, if anything, you did with the witness statements that you were provided with?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, I was, when I went through this material, I was not very clear how important these were, so I really read them page by page. And these were binders, a lot of material. And I -- in my first statement I also relied to them, but I was then told that this written -- witness statements were not as important as the military documents. So I had them in the back of my mind, knowing what went on in Dusina, in Maljine, in Miletici. But I did not go much deeper then when I went through the whole material for the second and finally the third time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I take it from the last comment that you made, the second and finally the third time, that your report has evolved over time.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes. It's an iterative process which had to be amended based on additional questions asked to me and based also by the incorporation of additional material provided to me, which basically caused me to go through the whole process again and see how this additional material would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. match what I have already worked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In addition, would it be correct to say that as a result of, for example, an order by the Trial Chamber, you made certain deletions from your report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I made deletions because I incorporated something which was given to me and in hindsight it seems that this was not the appropriate way, so I had to delete this again and had to rewrite and adapt this part of -- well, this was a larger part of my statement, obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General, as recently as two weeks ago -- or I should start back. On the 19th of April, sir, of this year, we had a meeting where we discussed your report and your testimony here today; is that -- do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at that meeting one of the things that we talked about was a number of the footnotes of your report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall or can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what we discussed with respect to the footnotes or some of the footnotes of your report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, my main problem was that from the first time I got these documents until the time I edited or wrote my paper, I had four different numbers -- types of numbers of individual documents. And by translating them back and forth, I had made some mistakes, because I'm not the greatest typist. I mixed up some things, and therefore I also ask you to help me to straighten this out, because I also lost two or three documents which I could not retrieve from my 23 binders. So this was the thing to straighten things out where I was not quite sure which was the appropriate number or where I just have written down a wrong number and couldn't find the right one. And I was helped by you to get the appropriate documents straightened out again in the proper sequence for the footnotes. I think these were about 15 or 16 footnotes where I still had troubles, which some of them I already indicated beforehand, which I found out, but about seven to eight I couldn't straighten out again, and I'll just ask for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General, during that meeting that we had, can you describe for the Trial Chamber what process you went through to verify the documents that you cited in your report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, some, as I just said, I had some question marks on very few footnotes, which I brought forward in an email to the Prosecution, asking me to provide me with the material which I had lost, especially when I destroyed the folder of the Blaskic case where some other documents were attached to. I asked them to replace them for me, to send them back, and I also asked to help me and find out the appropriate numbers of those documents. And when I came here, we finally -- I told you where my -- what my document numbers were and then we basically checked this together and realised that I was on the right track again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, earlier this afternoon, I showed you a filing that we had filed, a chart updating your report. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There was one instance in that report where the Prosecutor had made a change which we didn't discuss on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes. And this was right so, because I made a mistake there, referring it to a case, 18th April, to a case which happened six years -- six days later. So it was appropriate just to delete this reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, sir, would it be correct to state that having looked at the materials the Prosecution filed on the 22nd of April of this year that your report is now complete and as up to date as possible?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes. And we discussed that. I asked you to make these amendments in the footnotes because I was just not -- I just didn't have the capability to rewrite the whole thing again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, do you have any rough approximation as to the number of hours or number of days that you have spent reviewing this material and producing your expert report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No. I really don't. I never figured out how many days it was all together, but I tell you, it was much, much more time than I ever anticipated when I told Mr. Withopf that I would become his expert. If I had known this now from now, I would never have agreed upon that. Because it took much more time. My wife was very angry with me, because I was sitting days and nights just to scan all this material and to go through, it takes a hell of a time if it's a total new case, total new documents, and a topic you're not so familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like now to turn to your report. Do you have a copy of your report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I see also that you have actually two binders in front of you. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber what is contained in the two binders that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: In this binder I have my report, I have the comment of the Trial Chamber of changing some of the things, and I have all those different lists of the documents, the different numbers -- excuse me, the different numbers of the documents. And in this second binder, I have the documents referring -- to which I referred to in my footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I'm going to now ask you a few questions about each of the sections of your report. I'm going to do so in a slightly different order than you have presented the material. If you have any questions or if you don't understand what I'm asking you, please say so and I'll rephrase the question. I'd first like to turn to section 2 of your report, where you discuss the responsibility of a commander. General, can you please tell the Trial Chamber, briefly tell the Trial Chamber, what are the responsibilities of a military commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: The answer is rather simple, because the commander is responsible for everything which happens in the area he is responsible for, for which he takes command. So this is personnel, this is training, this is operations, this is morale and welfare, this is materiel, everything which affects his command, he is responsible for, and he's personally and uniquely responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what is the basis for command? What -- where does command come from?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, command is invested on you by higher headquarters, and it has different echelons. And you have to go through some particular training before you get this command to be capable of doing that, and then it's invested to you by your government, which has the trust that you would execute your commandship the appropriate way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, in your report, for example, on page 2, there are some footnote sources or footnote references to German regulations. Can you tell the Trial Chamber why your report begins with discussion of German regulations?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, I'm obviously more familiar with the German regulations than with the regulations of any other countries, and I also made reference to a book where all the different NATO regulations were brought forward and compared. And I realised that what I had as legal -- no, as written material was more consistent for me as far as the German regulations were concerned than, for instance, the British, the French, or the Americans, which I didn't have at my disposition by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In other paragraphs in section 2 of your report, you also make reference to JNA, that is, Yugoslav People's Army, regulations. Did you in fact compare those regulations with the German regulations you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I did this with the JNA regulations, which applied to a large extent also to the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was striking to me that they were very modern as far as the legal disposition was concerned, very similar, and if I had not known that before, it was obvious for me that the basic content of commandship of being a commander and the responsibility being uniquely responsible for what happens in your area of responsibility is very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you also, sir, look at any regulations pertaining specifically to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes. The ones which were in my papers I looked through. And again, besides using JNA declaration -- laws and rules, there were clear new rules, regulations, laws for the Bosnian army. And what I just said applied also to them. If I see the rules of the international law of war by the ABiH, this could have been written the same way, I think, in my country. It's very modern, it's very up to the requirements of today, and I don't see any big difference from what I used to work with in NATO countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about the role of a commander with respect to good order and discipline within the units that that commander has under his or her authority?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I think there are two aspects to this point as far as my answer is concerned. One is the commander is responsible, legally responsible, for discipline and order within his area of responsibility, and there's a law which binds him to do that and take care that no wrong things happen. On the other hand, it's also his personal interest that law and order prevails, because that is a key factor for the combat value of his forces. If his forces lose law and order, if they lose discipline, normally they become not such a combat-ready and trustful unit as he wants to have them, and then it's much more difficult for him to execute his power over those soldiers. So it's in his inherent interest that discipline is prevailed and ensured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, what duty or duties does a commander have once that commander issues an order?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Issuing an order is a - especially in military operations - a very complex endeavour, but issuing an order is not enough. You have to ensure afterwards that the order has been executed the way you want it executed. I mean, the control factor in the decision cycle, decision, appreciation of the situation, giving orders, and the last part of this decision cycle, then, is to make sure that the things really have been executed the way you want to, or if not, to make the appropriate amendments. So yes, control is a key thing in giving orders, and only by controlling this, you know that the things really have been executed that you want to have executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, you've told us you have to ensure afterwards that the order has been executed the way you want it executed. How does a commander do that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: There are also different ways. One way is, which we know from the old time, that the commander is sitting on the strategic point from which he overviews the whole battlefield as I see it right now and gives his direct order to influence what happens on the battle. So he can influence the battle directly. This is today not the way we do any more with high technical things. You send orders, you give -- you receive messages constantly from the battlefield, giving you an appreciation what's going on there. And based on that appreciation, you try to influence with your own messages, with your own additional orders, the flow of action going on on the battlefield. So this is a constant interrelation between the lower headquarters and the higher headquarters that you realise what's going on there. And the ideal thing is that you give an order and the execution will follow your order the same way and you don't have to interfere. But if necessary, you would interfere and today you would interfere by giving written or oral orders by telephone, by radio, or what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What are the duties of a commander with respect to information flows?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Information is always -- information flow a thing which goes from higher headquarter to lower headquarter. The higher headquarter has to establish the technical installations to lower headquarter so that the lower headquarter can report to the higher headquarter. And I think this prevails almost in all armies. So as a brigade commander, you have to ensure that you have technical facilities that you can talk to the battalions and the battalion can talk to you. The battalion commander has the same vis-a-vis the companies. So the battalion -- the commander, no matter what level he is, is responsible for establishing the communications, and if they're inadequate, he has to improve them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it from your description that this communication flow is a two-way street?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: It's a two-way street but the responsibility for the establishment of the technical facilities is for the higher headquarters. May I give an example to that? When I deployed to Kosovo, my former headquarters redeployed with all their equipment, as far as command and control, radios, and so on was concerned. So I had to rebuild the whole architecture of new command and control structures, including all the technical facilities from scratch, otherwise I wouldn't have been capable to commanding my forces, and my forces would not have been capable to exchange their information to forward this to me. So this was my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I'd like to turn your attention now to those sections within section 2 of your report, where you talked about disciplinary structures within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you recall the conclusions that you reached about the disciplinary structures and the court structures within the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, the disciplinary structure again are in consonance with the level of command. The higher the level of command, the broader the disciplinary possibilities of reaction for the commanders are there, and they are set down in a document which is called the rules of military discipline. And in a manual on military discipline, the details are laid out very similar, I would say, very similar to the ones familiar to me in my German army. In addition to that, there is a military -- there is a special military courts. There were military courts for the individual corps, one or two courts to which the commander could transfer those cases which basically surpassed his own capability as a disciplinary power, which were basically deeds which a court had to take care of, and again this has been regulated in a very detailed way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What are the responsibilities of commanders within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with respect discipline, based on the material that you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: He had to ensure discipline within his units. He had to ensure that the rules of the international military law have been adhered to. And it's obvious and very striking how often in different Official Gazettes, papers, laws, this comes up to. And he had to transfer the case to the court if he thought that the case in question would not be adequate for his level of disciplinary power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I'd like you to turn now, please, to paragraph 2.20 in your report. It's on page 6 in the English version. The final sentence of that paragraph concludes with footnote 24. Do you recall writing this part of your report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The first sentence of footnote 24 says: "This is exactly what Hadzihasanovic did." Do you recall what that was in reference to, what you were describing in that footnote?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic was not very happy about the slow reaction of the court. There were cases, obviously, at the court, and he was complaining that he didn't get the answers in time in order to proceed those cases, and because of that, he basically asked to do more on this. And he wrote that he was not very happy with those organs because they did not do the job as he expected them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General, do you recall, or if need be you can refer to the document, but if you recall, what type of crimes or offences was the accused Hadzihasanovic referring to in the document that you've cited to in this footnote? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, I think he did not refer to any very particular things, not any particular cases. I only refer that these were cases affecting the discipline within his forces, and he was very much concerned because by having a negative discipline, also the combat power of his forces would deteriorate. So it was in his interest that these cases would be solved, and as an example, to maybe prevent other soldiers doing similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I guess perhaps my question wasn't specific, but do you recall -- you've said that these cases were affecting discipline within his forces. What kind of cases were these?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: The cases are not enumerated in detail, but as far as disciplinary cases in this particular case, I think it was plundering. It was also leaving the forces unauthorised, going home, things of this kind of nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to turn now to section 3 of your report, and particularly paragraphs 3.2 and 3.3. You discuss the 3rd Corps of the ABiH and the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in those two paragraphs. Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what conclusions you reached about the establishment of those two units.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, the corps has established by the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it basically comprised the territorial forces in that area, to have one responsible for that. And these forces then were extended, additional forces were added to those, and the 7th Mountain Brigade, the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, was one of those brigades established in this area and attached to the 3rd Corps, a situation which I think was very difficult because there was no corps headquarters at the beginning. These were territorial forces at the beginning who had to be worked into a fighting force. A very difficult organisational, very difficult endeavour for the corps, as well as for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I'd like to turn to paragraph 3.5 of your report. In that paragraph, you discuss the leadership within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what conclusions you reached about the leadership of that brigade based on the documents you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: There was a brigade commander, Mr. Asim Koricic, who basically was appointed as a brigade commander, and he had a Chief of Staff in his brigade, Mr. Kubura. The brigade commander during that time when Mr. Kubura was his Chief of Staff, was absent for quite a while. And in that time, the deputy -- actually, the second highest ranking officer in the brigade, which is the Chief of Staff, took over command for those forces in the 7th Mountain Brigade, and at the end he then became the brigade commander of this brigade, after he had served for a couple of months as the Chief of Staff and for a certain period of time as the de facto brigade commander, but not the de jure brigade commander, because the de jure one was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, to your knowledge, and based on your experience in the military, what difference exists between, as you've called it, a de facto commander and a de jure commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, the one who is in the position to take over the command for a certain period of time, even so he is not the commander appointed, is, as far as the responsibility, the same situation. He is responsible for that period of time. He might not be appointed as a commander, but he is the commander with all the command and control relationship and responsibility as the commander who is not here by that period of time. That's the reason why you have somebody replacing him, with the same spectrum as the normal commander would have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, this would -- what you've described for us would necessarily follow, based on a principle of unity of command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber what unity of command refers to?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: The key thing is that you have one who is responsible for everything, which happens in that -- in his area of command. So that you don't split it. Therefore, in many armies, you have an authorised deputy, who then takes over if the commander goes. If you don't have a deputy, then the next high-ranking officer automatically takes over and takes the duties the commander would normally have. And I think this was the case here. But it was a rather long time for the Chief of Staff to take over as a commander, an exceptionally long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I'd like to turn now to paragraph -- or paragraphs 3.6 and the following paragraphs where you discuss the Operational Group Bosanska Krajina [sic]. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, based on the documents that you have read, what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: This operational group is a thing which other armies also create once in a while, what we would call a task force, where you have different forces subordinated under one intermediate commander, to coordinate in a certain area for a certain specific mission and for a certain period of time operations for the higher headquarters. So this is an intermediate headquarters responsible with a very small staff to coordinate this, because the higher headquarters cannot do this on the spot and cannot command and control all the forces directly. So this is an ad hoc situation which you would normally create a situation like this in the former Yugoslav army and I would say also in the Warsaw Pact countries. This, in NATO country, ad hoc situation, was established for a longer duration, and it was some intermediate command and control installation which seems to be playing to the variety of forces within this large corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it, sir, based on what you've told us, that there was nothing particularly unusual about the establishment of the OG Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No. And this was not the only one in the corps area. There were different -- there were additional ones. And in the other corps you also had operational groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What effect, if any, did the establishment of the operational groups have on the chain of command from the 3rd Corps to the units that were assigned temporarily to the OG?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, you had incorporated an additional layer of responsibility. So the responsibility for the corps -- from the corps commander did not go directly to the brigade commander but through the commander of the OG, and the same vice versa. But nevertheless, the brigade was always still under the command and control of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I'd now like to turn to section 5 of your report, beginning on page 14. You discuss in that section professionalism within the 3rd Corps. Can you highlight some of your findings with respect to the professionalism of the 3rd Corps, based on all of this material that you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think one has to say that for the leaders in the new Bosnian army, it was a very, very difficult job to build up an army not under peace conditions but under very adverse conditions, fighting with their former colleagues, fighting against the Serbs, and then against the Bosnian Croats at the same time, not having an established corps of officers, NCOs, as we have them in the West, trained, specifically trained and prepared for this kind of command and control relationship. So they had to do it out from scratch, with all the problems affected to that, that many things were not as solid as much based on professional knowledge and especially professional experience as you would expect it in a headquarter or a staff like this. In addition, I think the problem is that the materiel at the beginning was scarce materiel, practically materiel which has been taken over from the former Yugoslav army. But the key problem is that the leading officers of this new army had to jump into positions for which they were not prepared the same detailed way you normally would prepare them, by getting up step by step until they reach this level. They had to take up command responsibilities two to three levels higher than they were trained for, and therefore it was very, very difficult to do that at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, how did these difficulties manifest themselves with respect to issues surrounding command and control within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: It shows, for instance, that competent officers - and the most competent officers seem to have been the former Yugoslav -- the former officers of the Yugoslav army - were a scarce resource. Brigades were complaining they did not have proficient officers enough. They were complaining that the officers - especially on the platoon and company level - did not know their job adequately enough. They were complaining about the logistical differences. The command and control, as far as the technical equipment was concerned, was a problem. It was not state of the art, as you would expect it in a modern army. And all technical facilities were [Realtime transcript omitted the word "were"] used just to establish command and control. So in this regard, I think there was a lot of improvisation, I could imagine, in this army, a lot of improvisation to meet the criteria of building up the corps and at the same time of fighting the enemy in the whole area. This again was not an area where they had a clear-cut front line in which you attacked or over which attacked with corps level forces. These were all smaller battles conducted by the corps in the whole area, so there was never a real time to relax and to do the normal military training and business as you would do in any pauses. They were under constant pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that on page 35, line 22, there is a word which doesn't appear in the transcript. When the witness said, and I'll quote the witness: "And all technical facilities used just to establish command and control." In my opinion, Mr. President, the witness said: "And all technical facilities were used just to establish command and control." Could we confirm, Mr. President, that this word is missing from the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Did the witness say "were used," or something else? General, in the transcript, as the Defence has pointed out, in line 22, the term "used" appears. But you apparently said "were used." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, these difficulties that you've described with respect to the conclusions you've reached, did they continue throughout 1993? What was the time period of these difficulties you've described?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I think they continued throughout 1993. This was also the time period I was asked to look for. They may have improved in this or that case, but it seems that this was a major problem throughout the time of operations in that particular year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did these difficulties, sir, mean that the 3rd Corps was unable to function as a cohesive military unit?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, sir. It made it more difficult. The corps had clear communication establishments. It has a communication officer in the corps who basically coordinated everything as far as communication was concerned. The problems I'm referring to are more on the tactical level of companies and battalions basically in operations against an enemy who did not have the modern equipment they would normally appreciate it to have. They had outmoded equipment. And because of that, also security, as far as command and control was concerned, was very often jeopardised. The relations between the brigades and the corps, as far as I can deduct from all the documents I have looked through, were on the regular basis. There were regular messages from the brigades to the corps during operations. Even every six hours they were asked for and they were sent by the brigade commanders. So the basic operational knowledge of what happened on the battlefield was available for the commanding general of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, my final question before we take the break: What was -- with respect to these difficulties you've described, what was the overall effect of these difficulties on the functioning of the corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I think the corps as such could function appropriately, but the operations on the tactical level, as I just mentioned, were hampered and were maybe not so easy to conduct as they would have been conducted if they had had normal modern communication equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. President, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have the break now. It's a quarter to 4.00. And we will resume at about a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, we start the session. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, I'd now like to turn to sections 6 and 7 of your report, dealing with legal principles and legal responsibilities for ABiH commanders. Sir, in drafting these two sections of your report, what materials did you rely upon?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: There are the legal documents, like the decree of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the manual of service of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the rules of the international law of war by the ABiH, the order of enforcement of international military law, the decision to declare state of war, the manual on military discipline, the rules of military discipline, the law on special military courts, the statutory order of district military courts, plus the laws and manual applicable from the JNA, like the rules of land forces corps, the regulations of the authority of the ground forces corps commander, the Criminal Code of the SFRY, and the regulations on the application of the rules of international law of armed forces of the SFRY. These were the main documents. But I must tell you that I didn't have the entire documents. I always had paragraphs or articles of them, not the entire documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General, you certainly are not a professionally trained lawyer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I think this is very important to mention. I'm a professional soldier, but not a professional lawyer. This has not been the main topic of my former job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Nevertheless, can you tell the Trial Chamber what type of training or education you might have received concerning the law as it relates to military issues and the conduct of hostilities during your military career?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: First of all, as a young officer candidate, you learn everything about disciplinary rights and the soldiers' law in which the boundaries, the legal boundaries of your profession are established. So you learn how to conduct a disciplinary [indiscernible], how to investigate, how to turn to a court if necessary, through a divisional headquarters. This is the one in the German army which basically has this right to turn to the court. These things are being taught to you at the school, at the officers candidate school. And then you go on to become a battalion commander, you get additional information on that. The very key question is the question on the Geneva Convention, the question on international military law and human rights, which are being trained again and again. And let me tell you: Before we are deployed to all our peacekeeping operations, especially the later parts of my answer, became very obviously a key feature which we discussed with our soldiers before we deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, General, as a result of this periodic training you received in your military career, you were certainly familiar with some of the fundamental tenets of international law and the law of armed conflict. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I would say, so yes, sir. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And would the same conclusion be true with respect to general notions or basic principles of military criminal justice?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: As far as the military criminal justice is concerned, I think I'm not as familiar, because normally things of military criminal justice are being transferred to courts. And I never had any direct connection with the court, because it never happened in my career that I had to deal with problems like this. Therefore, I know they are there. I know, I think, the basic principles, how they would be applied, but I have no whatsoever personal experience in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the role or responsibilities of a military commander in the military criminal justice system that you were familiar with, can you tell the Trial Chamber what those basic principles were? What were the primary responsibilities of a military commander with respect to military justice?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, whenever there was a criminal injustice been committed to which the commander thought his disciplinary right would be expended, that these disciplinary possibilities would not be adequate, and if a capital activity has happened, then he had to turn this case to the court, and it was then being conducted in front of a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us, based on your experience, training, background, and the review of the materials that the Office of the Prosecutor provided to you, can you compare what you were experienced with or familiar with as a result of your training with the documents from either the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the army of BiH, or even the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I want to reiterate that I'm not an expert on that. But as far as I can deduct it from the documents I've seen and from my experience, I think the big difference is not in the handling of a commander. Once he knows the case, expands his capability, he then informs the court and gives the case and transfers the case to the court, I think the difference between the German system and the system you just mentioned in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also in the JNA, is that there is a military court. We don't have a military court in Germany. It goes to the normal civil court, and the civil court then presides the case because we have no military justice in this case in our country, based on our history. But the principle for the commander to take the case and to basically get all the material ready to transfer the case then to the appropriate corps, I think is basically the same. What happens then in the court is a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General, you just mentioned the principle for the commander to get all the material ready to transfer the case. What does that entail? What is that all about?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, he has to see what the case was -- who were and who were involved in the case, who were the possible perpetrators, what are the sources which still can be found, who are possible testimonies. So these are the things he has to ensure on the ground and get all this evidence ready to transfer it then to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, how would a commander do these things that you've just told us about, to get the case ready to transfer to a court? What are his obligations?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, there are a variety of organisations, installations helping him to do that, because he normally wouldn't go where the crime has happened. He would have his security forces and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He would send his military police. He would also have his legal experts on the staff, specially trained for this kind of evidence-gathering and for initiating the case. So in the German army, I would have turned this to my legal advisor, and my legal advisor would have started investigation on my behalf. He would inform me how the case would being succeeded or not. But basically it would be his job on my behalf to do that. And there were legal -- there was a legal division in the corps headquarters in the Bosnian army as well where you had legal professionals to look for these things and to do the job for the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, I'd now ask you to turn to section 4 of your report, which is on page 9 of the English version. You've entitled this section, "Subordination of the Mujahedin within the 3rd ABiH Corps." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what materials you relied upon in writing this section of your report.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: These are orders by the commanding general of the 3rd Corps to his subordinate brigades. These are orders, internal reports of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade about events that happened within the brigade sector. These are reports and excerpts of war diaries of the 306th Mountain Brigade, which to some extent cooperated together with the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade and Mujahedin in operations. This is a text of a Muslim video, or Mujahedin video, where the Mujahedin portrayed themselves in their history of Mujahedin in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So these are all, with the exception to the video, military documents of different levels in the 3rd Corps sector, under which I -- on which I based my assumptions here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General, you mentioned videotape. Did you in fact watch this videotape?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, sir. I just said: These were the texts, the transcripts. I didn't see the videotape itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: But if I may expand. It shows how the Mujahedin saw themselves in that area also vis-a-vis the military environment in which they operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Another -- sir, I forgot to ask you this question, but another overarching factor that I think is important: The documents, all of the documents that you have been provided with, what language were those documents in?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: All these language are translations in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, General, just for the record, you do not read the B/C/S or Serbo-Croat language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like you to turn in the English version of your report to page 10 and look at paragraphs 4.5 and 4.6. Those two paragraphs, sir, at first glance or at first reading, might not be consistent. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how those two paragraphs can be reconciled, or how you reached those conclusions that you set forth in those two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, the problem is the documents I had are not giving very clear indication. You only can make deductions and assumptions based on the military experience one has, how it could have been. Because there is no clear order where it says the Mujahedin or a group of Mujahedin belonged to the 7th Mountain Brigade. I haven't found anything like this. But I found quite a few documents where a cooperation in operations or a complaint after operations about the behaviour of the Mujahedin within the area of the 7th Mountain Brigade or the 306th Mountain Brigade, are so obvious that there must have been some cooperation beforehand, otherwise they wouldn't have been in the area, otherwise the commander or his responsible [sic] for the morale and welfare would not complain about the misbehaviour of the Mujahedin within their area. So if they cooperated to some way there must be some kind of cooperation, some kind of way of preparing operations, of conducting operations. This was just not a very loose things going totally independently. And therefore, it's very difficult that you don't have a paper in which you can say: Here on the paper it says they were part of this or that battalion. On the other hand, they spearheaded and advanced in the operation with the battalions in operations. And therefore, there must have been a cooperation, because they just do [sic] it on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General, you tell us that there must have been cooperation. What do you base that on? What is the basis for saying there must have been cooperation?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, if I see the report of the brigade commander of his battalions, and he reports that in his 1st Battalion there is this company and that company, and he says in addition, "I have 60 to 70 Arabs," which are Arabs/Turks, which is the expression for the Mujahedin, then it shows that these Arab/Turks were somehow involved in the daily life of the battalion. The same goes for the 2nd Battalion.
