It also shows that an officer responsible for the security of the brigade went into a battalion sector after an operation and complains very much about the negative behaviour, the chaos [Realtime transcript read in error "caste"] which has been established by the Mujahedin within that area. So I think one can deduct that if they operated with them in the area and created chaos afterwards, they must have been a part of that. In addition, coming back to the video, it says very clearly in the video that they offered training to the battalion, to one of the battalions of the 7th Mountain Brigade, and I think training is a part of cooperation, at least in the way I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, just a couple of follow-on or clarification questions, if I may. Again on the transcript before you, you'll see page 44, line 25, and page 45, line 1, you said: "And therefore there must have been a cooperation, because they just do it on their own."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: They just don't do it on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just don't do it on their own. And also, two places in the last answer that I think the transcript misstated. Did you make reference to chaos being established by the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: At least that's what the text says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me again draw your attention to paragraph 4.6. You say there are some traceable indications that individual Mujahedin were serving with and in the 7th MMB already in early 1993. What do you base that conclusion on?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I base it on the conclusion that internal reports of the 7th Brigade complain in the aftermath of operations about the behaviour of the Mujahedin, who - and I assume this then - had to have been members of the operation before. There is a document where it's clearly said that this close cooperation is a moral factor for the battalion, the 1st Battalion of the 7th Mountain Brigade, working so closely with the Mujahedin which boosts up the morale of their own soldiers. So if they have not cooperated, why having that boosting factor of those forces? So I think one can deduct from the way that these forces, as I also said before, were included in the enumeration of a battalion commander that in addition to his companies, there are 60 to 70 Turks/Arabs or Arabs/Turks, that this is not just without any kind of cooperation. I don't know exactly how deep this cooperation was. I don't know how many Mujahedin who basically trained also the so-called guerrilla were leading or part of the guerrilla, but at least there was a close rapport, because if you train them, you have to cooperate with them. And it says that they spearheaded some of the operations, that they were advancing before the other operations happened. So if as a military, if I imagine an operation being conducted, you normally don't have a spearhead unit or an advancing unit with whom you don't cooperate in detail just in order to prevent fratricide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, what would be the result, if you will, of this cooperation with respect to command and control issues? What is the relationship between what you've described as cooperation and command and control?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: If I conducted an operation, I'm responsible for everything which happens within that cooperation, within that operation. So I'm responsible for what happens there, for the positive as for the negative points of the operation, because this is my command responsibility. In forces who work with me in this regard, in an operation, in an area of responsibility for which I'm responsible, fall then automatically also in my responsibility as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, did you see any legal documents, regulations, laws, et cetera, provided to you by the Office of the Prosecution that would support the notion that you've just described for us?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, I did not. And maybe there is none, because the first official paper in this regard is the paper by the commanding general of the 3rd Corps asking for the possibility to build up an organic unit of the Mujahedin. So this organic unit, this build-up, the organisational order for the build-up of the organic unit shows that he was not very happy with the situation until that time. I haven't, at least I -- in the documents provided to me, I haven't found any official document in this regard where I could deduct they were part of -- an original part like a unit of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think, sir, my previous question perhaps wasn't clear. I'd like to return to that. You told us about a commander being responsible for everything that happens within an operation. Did you see any documents, regulations or legal documents, codes, et cetera, that would support the notion that an ABiH commander is responsible for everything that happens within an operation?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think in Article 21 of the regulations on the applications of the rule of international war of the armed forces of the SFRY, which was also applicable for the Bosnian forces, it says that the commander is responsible for what happens in his area. Even so, they are not elements of his own forces, but working with him, cooperating with him in this area, he takes automatically responsibility for these things being happening -- that happen in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, General Reinhardt, do you recall discussing this provision anywhere in your report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall which paragraph or paragraphs you might have discussed this provision?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, I just have to look right now. Excuse me. I have now to look a little bit. It's paragraph 4.22. But as we discussed it earlier last -- when I was here 14 days ago, the reference was wrong. It's not -- it's not the reference as I pointed out in footnote 78, but the one I just mentioned before. And I think I also mentioned it in paragraph 9, or in chapter 9, but I don't know right now which under 9 it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. But you do discuss it in paragraph 4.22 of your report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, let me then return to the subject that we touched on, and I've just got a few more questions for you, sir. Did there come a time when the Mujahedin were consolidated within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes. There was obviously a time, because the commanding general asked the headquarters of his forces to bring them into an organic unit, to form an organic unit of the Mujahedin, and to put them under his command. And on 13 August, they were established as an organic El Mujahedin unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which year was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, based on your review of the documents and your interpretation of those documents based on your experience, why was this unit established?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I think there are two reasons. One reason is - at least, this is what the corps commander reported to higher headquarters - that he didn't want to be further accountable for what happens in his area of responsibility by Mujahedins under which he did not have constant and direct control, and therefore, he said, "Let's put them into a unit and then it's easier for me." And the other thing is, if I deduct it from the transcript of the video, that the Mujahedin themselves were not very happy with their situation, and somehow they refused to continue to cooperate fighting with the Bosnian army as long as they would not be put into a direct -- in a state of a direct unit of the 3rd Corps. So they themselves also asked for becoming a unit within the Bosnian army. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, can you elaborate upon what you just told us when you said the corps commander did not have constant and direct control over the Mujahedin. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: That's what we just discussed before, that the Mujahedin were operating in his area of responsibility, but not as you would have a normal unit, with direct control and effective control over them, but only part time they were working with his units. And some might have been included in his units. Some kind might have just cooperated. And therefore, it was more difficult for him to take disciplinary command and control and charge them for the misbehaviour than if they were an organic unit. So the situation was more loose for him, more difficult to execute his disciplinary power and his command and control over these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, could you please turn now to section 8 of your report on page 21 in the English version. Based on your review of the documents that were provided to you, can you tell the Trial Chamber what conclusions you reached about the notice that might have reached the accused with respect to events described and alleged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, the first documents I found were documents of early February, which seemed to me to be a consequence of what happened in Dusina, because the French General Morillon asked the commanding general of the 3rd Corps to come and have a discussion with him. And right after this, the commanding general issued an order to his brigade commanders, telling them to, I would say, very simple, to behave properly, according to the law. And two days later, he issued another order to all brigade commanders, telling them, "We don't want to be as the other side is. We want to show that we are better, that we are better prepared and that we are fighting according to the human law." And he made the brigade commanders responsible that if their soldiers don't adhere to the Geneva Convention, that he would make them responsible and that the brigade commanders had to make their soldiers responsible. So there was a clear reaction in the way as the law provides it for in the ABiH that he basically monitored his commanders to do that. He does it again in April. He does it again in June. So there are many written orders to the brigade commanders in which he complains about the misbehaviour of individual soldiers and admonishes his commanders to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, what is the temporal relationship between these written orders that you've just referred to and the crimes alleged in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: You cannot relate all the things which I just discussed to criminal activities as related in the indictment. But Dusina for me is pretty clear, that Dusina, which happened on the 26th of January, and the reactions which I just mentioned on the 1st and 3rd February, seem to be related. And I think again to what I have seen from Miletici, which was the 306th Brigade, together with elements of the 7th Mountain Brigade, and the reactions on that, again is a clear idea that something has happened here. And again with the Guca Gora complex, the commander basically admonishes his troops that they have to stop things which they have done here. And Maljine again, when Maljine happened, very shortly afterwards you see those kinds of orders. So there's for me a clear action and reaction of the commanding general telling his forces that what they have done was not the right way to do it, and monitoring them that they should not do this and making their commander responsible for what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Finally, General, if you could turn please to section 9 of your report, dealing with the actions taken by the accused. Again, based on your experience and background and the documents that you've reviewed, can you tell us what steps the accused Hadzihasanovic took with respect to notice of these crimes that you've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I might reiterate myself now a little bit, but he has published and issued written orders in which he made clear that he knows about criminal activities, that he doesn't accept them, that he admonishes his commanders that they prevent their soldiers from looting, plundering, killing, mistreating civil citizens, priests, destroying churches, and making the brigade commanders responsible that their soldiers act accordingly. And that goes like a red thread from February to June. And in this regard, the commanding general of the corps shows a clear reaction to what have happened on the battlefield. In one case, in Kakanj, where the 3rd Battalion of the 7th Mountain Brigade was looting and destroying property of the civilian population, he even ordered the brigade commander of the 7th Mountain Brigade to relieve the battalion commander and company commanders, so this is a very clear, outspoken order to his subordinate, but I don't know whether the execution really has taken place of the relief of those officers, of those commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, the event you've just described in Kakanj, you make reference to that in your report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would you characterise that incident as being one in which the commander took the appropriate steps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I think the commanding general is very clear and very strong here, telling his brigade commander, "I'm not happy with what had happened here. Your commanders were responsible for that, and I expect you to relieve them. No, I don't expect you. I order them. I order you to relieve them." I think this is the reaction which I would have expected in my army, that if a commander -- or if the troops of a commander misbehaved the way they did, that you relieve the commander right away and start then afterwards an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, based on your review of the materials provided to you, on how many other occasions did the corps commander take similar steps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I really don't know. This is the only document which I found in the stack of documents provided to me. There might have been different cases, but this is the only one which I have found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you find any similar instances of situations where the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, the accused Kubura, took similar steps with respect to subordinate units under his command?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not. Again, also the brigade commander of the 7th Mountain Brigade gave orders to his subordinate battalions to discontinue looting and plundering and things like that. But I haven't seen any case in which he took additional measures than those. And there's a particular case in Vares where his neighbouring brigade commander accused him that the soldiers of the 7th Mountain Brigade misbehaved dramatically in the operations, but he just -- he just said, "These were not my soldiers." And he just denied it. So he did not went any further on those accusations of his fellow brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Reinhardt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this concludes examination-in-chief of this witness. I'm wondering if this would be the appropriate time to tender General Reinhardt's report into evidence or if Your Honours would prefer that that wait. We would certainly wish that to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now turn to the Defence. The Prosecution is requesting that the expert witness's report be admitted into evidence. What is the Defence's position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Our belief is that we should wait for the conclusion of the cross-examination in order to assess the probative value of this report and to take a decision with regard to the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will withdraw for a few minutes and we'll be back in a few minutes' time. We will now deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 5.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as tendering the expert witness's report into evidence, the Trial Chamber has taken note of the fact that the Prosecution has requested that this document be admitted into evidence. Defence counsel would rather wait for the cross-examination to be concluded. It is the Trial Chamber's opinion that, given that this is an expert witness's report and we are discussing questions of the admissibility at the moment, we can admit this report, and its probative value will be assessed at a subsequent date. Could Madam Registrar give us a number for this report now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit number is P108. It's five past 5.00 now. It's now possible to start with the cross-examination. We will work until a quarter to 6.00, since we have to work until 7:00 p.m. We'll then have a 25-minute break and continue until 7.00 p.m., after the break. Mr. Bourgon, you may start with your cross-examination. I assume that you have divided the task and that Mr. Dixon will cross-examine on behalf of the other accused. I don't know how you have organised yourselves on the basis of subjects or on the basis of days. Could you tell us how the defence intends to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have two different cross-examinations, one for the accused General Hadzihasanovic and another for the accused Mr. Kubura. As far as General Hadzihasanovic is concerned, whom I represent, the Defence intends to cross-examine the witness for about two hours, which we have already informed the Trial Chamber of. As we are discussing time, the Trial Chamber said that they would like to ask the witness questions on the last day, for about four hours. Since we have 20 hours of hearings during the week, I've spoken to my colleague, who represents Mr. Kubura, and we believe that if General Hadzihasanovic spends 12 hours and the Defence for Kubura spends about 12 hours [as interpreted] on cross-examining the witness, we should then have enough time for the Trial Chamber to ask the witness the questions it wants to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. You may take the floor for 12 hours now. Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic, on behalf of Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think there is a mistake in the transcript. Mr. Kubura's Defence will need two hours, not 12 hours for the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So Defence for General Hadzihasanovic will require 12 [sic] hours, six times two, and Mr. Kubura's Defence will require two hours, two times one, roughly speaking. The breaks have been included. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to start this cross-examination by showing a Defence exhibit. In order to explain this to the Trial Chamber, there is a map behind the witness. You have a map there, Mr. President. It was placed in the courtroom last week. You must have noticed it. And I would just like to refer to a document that mentions how this map was prepared. This map is a collage of documents we have already tendered. It is the series of maps on the scale of 1:25.000. We took the following exhibits: DH98, DH99, DH100, 101, 102, 103, 104, and 105. That makes up a total of eight maps, to which we have added eight -- I apologise, six other maps. We only have one copy of these maps. I will tender this document in order to illustrate what I am saying. Could the usher please distribute this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could, while this document is being passed around. I notice from where I'm sitting it appears that there are some markings in the upper left or central panel of this map, and I don't -- perhaps we could have an explanation as to what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon will explain that. Since the Judges don't have binoculars, and we would need military binoculars in order to read the indications from where we are sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my colleague is quite right. I can see the indications. I won't be using this map today, but I think I will take advantage of the cross-examination in order to explain to everyone where the map comes from. As you can see, Mr. President, together with the document that you have in front of you, you have in white, together with the numbers, indications for the maps that are on the table. And the maps which are shaded are new maps. We only have one copy. This provides us with a representation, the one we have there. The only map that is missing is the map in the upper left-hand corner. The Jajce 24 map, we weren't in a position to obtain it, and that's why we have a missing piece on the map in front of you, Mr. President. We intend to use the map when cross-examining the witness. I would also like to inform you, Mr. President, that on the back of this panel, we have maps 1 to 100.000, on a scale of 1:100.000 and 1:200.000. We made a collage in order to represent an entire sector, and we'll be referring to this map too. I have a similar document that I want to tender. I will do so when I turn this panel around tomorrow, and this relates to the maps on a scale of 1:100.000 and 1:200.000. And Mr. President, I will now commence with my cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Stefane Bourgon, and this afternoon I'm accompanied by my colleague Ms. Edina Residovic from Sarajevo and Ms. Muriel Cauvin from France. Together we represent General Hadzihasanovic in the course of this historical trial. I say historical, Mr. Reinhardt, because I think it is important that I start my questions by mentioning the fact that this is the first time since 1946 that a commanding general is accused solely on the basis of the manner in which he exercises command and the command he was entrusted with. Now, my question to you, sir, is that I take it that the Prosecution did inform you when preparing the expert report and that you agree that General Hadzihasanovic did not commit any crimes himself in Bosnia in 1993. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it, Mr. Reinhardt, that you would also agree with me that General Hadzihasanovic did not order the commission of any crimes in Central Bosnia in 1993. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I agree. Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you also agree, Mr. Reinhardt, that General Hadzihasanovic did not plan the commission of any crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you also agree, Mr. Reinhardt, that General Hadzihasanovic did not instigate the commission of any crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Reinhardt, I take it, and I would understand that you would agree with me that General Hadzihasanovic did not aid or abet in any way in the commission, the ordering, the planning, or the instigating of any crime in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree, Mr. Reinhardt, that in all the material which has been given to you, and you have made reference to quite substantial Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. material, up to 23 binders of orders, of war diaries, and other similar documentation, plus one video that you say is not a military document, would you agree with me, Mr. Reinhardt, that in all this material that was given to you, you did not come across any evidence showing that General Hadzihasanovic had either committed, ordered, planned, instigated or aided and abetted in the commission of a crime in any way in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I haven't seen anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Reinhardt, you are probably quite aware that the charges in the indictment against General Hadzihasanovic focus on the allegations that he did not take reasonable and necessary measures to prevent the commission of crimes by his subordinates or to punish the perpetrators thereof. Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you aware that this is the first time since 1946 that charges are laid against a commanding general solely on the basis that he did not take reasonable and necessary measures to prevent his troops from committing crimes or to punish them for doing so?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Reinhardt, with a case, a war crimes trial which took place following World War II called Yamashita case?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to show you a quote from the judgement that was rendered in the Yamashita case. I would like -- [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender this document into evidence. I have copies for everybody, and I would like them to be distributed in the courtroom. There's just one quote from this judgement. [In English] If you can please read this citation from the Yamashita judgement. Now, Mr. Reinhardt, I was under the impression, and of course I may be wrong, that this was a very famous quote that was used in the training of a lot of commanders in many armies in the world. But maybe you have never been made aware of this quote in Germany?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, reading from this quote, Mr. Reinhardt, and of course I would like to ask you to look at this quote not from a legal perspective but from a command perspective. And I think it is necessary to read out loud this quote.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May it be noted that the interpreters do not have this quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... "a murderer or rapist because one of his soldiers commits a murder or a rape. Nonetheless, where murder and rape and vicious revengeful actions are widespread offences," and I stress here the words "vicious, revengeful actions, which are widespread offences," "and there is no effective attempt...", again, I stress the word "no effective attempt," "by a commander to discover and control the criminal acts, such a commander may be held responsible, even may be criminally liable, for the lawless acts of his troops." Would you agree with this quote, Mr. Reinhardt?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I therefore take it that you agree that from a command perspective that even if a commanding general did not order the commission of a crime but if his subordinates do actually commit vicious, widespread offences and that if he does nothing, then he may be responsible and even criminally liable for the acts of his subordinates. Would you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in this case, Mr. Reinhardt, and I quote here from paragraph 9.2 of your report, which is on page 24. Here I have the words that you used at paragraph 9.2, in the middle of the paragraph, where you say: "They felt responsible for incidents in their areas of responsibility and they tried to stop these from happening by issuing pertinent written orders." These are your words that you wrote yourself?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I further quote you at paragraph 10.1, on page 28. That's paragraph 10.1, and that is towards the end of the paragraph, where you say that: "In the wording of their many orders to their commanders, the accused were always very strong and outspoken." Those again are your words?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And today, in response to a question from my colleague from the Prosecution, and I refer the Trial Chamber to page 50, lines 19 to 24, again you mention that the accused General Hadzihasanovic issued many orders and that he monitored the actions of his subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So my question, based on what we have discovered, would I be right in saying that in your professional opinion, after reviewing all the material that you have been given, the issue in this case is not whether the accused took actions to prevent, because you just said that they did take actions to prevent, but the issue is whether they went the extra step to take actions to punish violations of international law. Is that a fair summary of your --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- opinion today? Now, we have heard and we have read also your numerous qualifications, and I would like to express on behalf of the Defence my appreciation to you for having accepted to take on this challenge and to be here today to share your knowledge with the parties and with the Trial Chamber. For me, Mr. Reinhardt, and I come to my question, you are not a Prosecution witness, but you are an expert witness whose duty it is to offer an objective opinion based on facts that were presented to you, without any bias to any of the parties. Would you agree with me that this is your duty as an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I also take it, Mr. Reinhardt, that you would agree with me that if during your testimony - and we will, of course, spend some time together this week. You've heard that we will have this conversation for some 12 hours or so - that if the evidence that comes out this week, if a different light is shed on the facts that you have been shown, or if you should be shown with new and additional information that you may not have been aware before coming here today, that, as an expert, you may be called upon to change your professional and objective opinion on your conclusions found in your report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I would like to do at this time, Mr. Reinhardt, is to explain to you how we will proceed for the next 11 or 12 hours or so, so that it is quite clear what -- and so that the Trial Chamber is well aware as to what I would like to get from you, and so then there is no confusion with respect to my colleagues from the Prosecution. The first thing I would like to do is to review with you some aspects of your qualifications, and my objective in doing so is to help the Trial Chamber to determine the extent to which your expertise will be helpful in deciding the issue in this case. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Secondly, in the second part of my cross-examination, I would like to ask you some questions on the role of a corps commander. As I'm sure you know, when a Trial Chamber authorise a party to call an expert witness, it is because the Trial Chamber believes that the witness has some specific knowledge which the parties don't have and which can help the Trial Chamber to analyse the evidence and decide on the issue. Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in this case, the Prosecution did not really inform us as to what your specific domain of expertise was, but of course we know from your background that you have detailed military knowledge. There can be no doubt about that. And as you've stated yourself, you've been a commander for most of your career and there can be no doubt about that. And it is our submission that the questions we will put to you have the objective of fulfilling the aim of an expert witness, and that is, to help the Trial Chamber to understand the issues, to understand the military situation, and to benefit from your expertise so that everyone in the courtroom can understand what really was going on and the situation in which General Hadzihasanovic exercised the command he was entrusted with. Is that your understanding of your role this week?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but I must tell you that I don't know everything which was going on, at least not in the military field. Because I am not an expert of the war on Bosnia-Herzegovina. I just looked into those cases, but I'm not a military expert in what was going on in the field, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These types of comments are helpful, because in all likelihood this is aimed at allowing the Judges to grasp what you can help them with and what may be something that you are less able to help. And all this is important in assessing the charges laid against General Hadzihasanovic. Now, as for the other issues, in terms of -- I was talking about your qualifications. We were not clear as to whether you possess the necessary qualifications to assist the Trial Chamber, and I quote specifically on legal issues and on issues related to Mujahedin. On the reading of your CV, we had some doubts. But this has been resolved, because the Trial Chamber has issued a ruling saying that you were qualified to speak about those issues. So my only question at this time is whether you feel that you are qualified and comfortable to provide an opinion on all the issues covered in your report.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: As far as the legal basis -- the legal documents I've been given, and as far as the questions asked to me I've been given, I feel qualified to give answers on that. But as I said before, I'm not a legal expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in the third and final part of my cross-examination, I will endeavour to cover some facts with you, some of which that you may be aware from reading the documents, some which, of course, may be new to you, because I will try to show you some documents that maybe were not found in the 23 binders that were given to you, and to ask you some specific questions. So quite easy. Part 1, your qualifications; part 2, we'll move into really benefiting, taking the most from your military experience; and part 3 we'll try apply this to the facts of the case. Now, before I begin with part 1, with the questions related to your qualifications, I need, before we start into this, to go into the preparation of your report and to the methodology that you used in preparing this report, so that we are -- we start from the same document. My first questions with respect to this -- to your report deals with the relationship that you have developed with the Prosecution while preparing your report and preparing to testify today. You mentioned, and I would like you to comment upon, a little earlier, in response to a question from my colleague, that this had developed into -- I'm not sure what the word [sic], but interrelation between yourself and the Prosecution in the development phase of your report. Could you elaborate on this for us, please.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes. The first step was that I was asked by Mr. Withopf to come to The Hague and discuss the basic issue of that case, to lay down the basic issue, and to look into documents in order to see whether I can understand the basic case. And then I was called back, discussing this case and some of the documents and was asked whether I would be willing to elaborate on what I had done as a first step. And I said, yes, I would. And then I was given a lot of material, went through the material, and made a first draft of a paper, based on questions which I have been given by that time. And then I came here again and I was given additional material, plus additional questions. And in this regard, I mean, there was some interrelation that I did my analysis, wrote it down, and came back here, and most of the time I've been then issued new material which I had to incorporate in order to rewrite my statement. And the last part was, as you know, that I had to take quite a few things out again of the report which I had already been given in here, and I was asked to come in here to get all this material and to crank it into the paper. So this was basically a continuation by editing or not -- editing is wrong, I'm sorry. By giving me, issuing me additional material which I had to then incorporate in the statement which I have already prepared until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Reinhardt, thank you very much for this quite thorough response. Could you inform the Trial Chamber whether in this process, how many different versions of your report were either given or looked at by the representatives of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I think it was five, but two were just because we had to renumerate the documents, because we had a different way of issuing the documents, and to rewrite it the appropriate way. So I think the papers which I brought in here from the first until the last one, which you have right now, actually are four different versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Reinhardt, I take it that the Prosecution were very clear in the questions that they put to you in terms of what they wanted from you, what questions they wanted answers to?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, they were very clear in the questions, but they were never very clear -- actually, they led me very far in the blind about their being satisfied with my work. Let me put it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. Could you elaborate a bit?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Okay. If you turn in a paper, normally you expect that the one who gets the paper somehow comments on the paper and says, okay. It's all right or not. I never got a comment on that. Because they said, "We are not entitled to tell you anything about the paper. We give you additional information. Please work it in." But we didn't talk about the substance, the quality of the paper which I have prepared. And that was at least for me not very easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And thank you very much for the response. Now, you mentioned that your first contact, the first phone call that you received, was some two years ago.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, I think it was one and a half year ago, somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One and a half years.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Because they also had to go to the minister of defence in Germany, from which I get the permission to come here, and I was asked to come here to do this kind of job, and that took quite a while, until we then really went into the actual business.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because if I recall correctly, you retired in April of 2001.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And so you were still a serving member when they contacted you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was a retired general by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you -- you mentioned that there was a process where there was an initial question concerning the Mujahedin and 7 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That was the first question that was put to you with some documents.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you recall for the benefit of the Trial Chamber the other questions that were put to you? Now, you've answered already that they relate to the subtitles in the report, but the order in which these questions came to you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I don't think I can really recall in detail about the order, because this was an evolving process. I remember that I was asked to elaborate what is a commander all about and what is the specific role in reference to a NATO commander and a commander of the Bosnian corps, are there any differences. We were discussing the question of disciplinary and legal issues as far as disciplinary is concerned, in comparison to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what I'm familiar with and what I found out in those papers, the legal responsibilities. But I cannot tell you the priority in which I got the questions. But the nine questions, and these are the ten is my summary, the nine questions were basically evolving over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the questions, sir, concerning the actions taken by General Hadzihasanovic, was that the last question or was that in the process? When did this become a command responsibility case in terms of your opinion?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: This was I think a very early question, because the case was against Hadzihasanovic and against Mr. Kubura and a third one by that time, and the question was: What did they know and how did they react.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you knew at that time when you began on this endeavour, or this project, that the indictment already existed and that both accused had already appeared before the ICTY? Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I knew about the indictment and the amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were these documents given to you so that you could know what these people were accused of?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So in focusing and in preparing your report, in addition to the questions by the Prosecution, you were also focusing on what the indictment was all about?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If I have just focused also on those cases only, and I come back to what I said before on the military operations, I didn't focus very much on the military operations because they were not the key questions I was asked for. This was just a background taken that this has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, did you receive any assistance from people? I mean, did you get help within Germany, private help? I'm not talking any link whatsoever with the Prosecution, but did you seek assistance? Sometimes consultants and experts seek assistance from other people to help them, because there was quite a volume of documents. Did you seek any assistance or did you get --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What kind of assistance did you --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: In the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Translation?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I have my translator from my former headquarters asking me -- asked him to help me in the translation, because my English, as you have realised this afternoon, is not good enough, not fluent enough, to prepare a paper which is rather consistent in your language.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, sir, if I spoke German as well as you spoke English, I would be very happy.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But it's -- so did you receive any other assistance in terms of other --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- translation from English to German?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, sir, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you did mention that you worked very long hours on this project.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And much more than what you envisaged at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you did not recall how many hours total, but I asked this information to the Prosecution earlier, which was not given to me, but how many hours were you actually paid to do this report? How many hours did they pay you? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: This is somewhere -- they are still -- some quite a few hours are still open. I don't know whether I'm paid for that or not. I'm sure I will. But, sir, I must tell you, I don't know. It was never a subject for me. For me it was a subject to eat myself [sic] through the documents and to get the proper information out in relation to my matrix, which concerned those questions. I only realised that it took much, much more time than I envisaged and it prevented me from doing many other things I wanted to do and I couldn't do because I was hooked up in this material, in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My aim was simply to try and put an objective figure.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I really don't know. I never thought about this before. I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you were actually going through the documents and also drafting the initial product that you were doing, did you seek at any time guidance from the OTP, from the Prosecution, because there's an issue that you did not understand or that there were additional documents that you were -- that you thought you required?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No. No, I never asked back on this one. Besides coming here and getting additional material, asking them to work this in, I got no additional guidance and I didn't call back for additional guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And now, we have, of course, your final report, which is the third one that we actually received. We received one in November; is that correct? And then there was a second one because you were asked to do some modifications. And that, I believe, came in January.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then this latest one, where you made some changes -- actually, you approved some changes that were made by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No. I made -- I made all the changes, with the exception of one. All the other changes were basically already indicated by me to Mr. Withopf in an email, and then when I came here, I had additional -- a handful of additional changes, because I was rather uncertain about the numbering of the documents, and I misplaced some documents in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go into some detail into the preparation and the documents, but for now I'd like to focus on the material which was given to you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to make a break now. It is a quarter to 6.00. We will resume at 10 past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Bourgon. Before that, I would like to invite you to, when responding, when you respond and when you hear the question, you turn towards the Chamber rather than towards the Defence counsel. And the second issue is: We are going to adjourn -- we are going to stop putting questions to you at 10 to 7.00 because we have some housekeeping matters to deal with. Without further ado, I'm giving the floor to Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Welcome back, Mr. Reinhardt.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We will now continue with my last question. Before I do raise this question, however, I've been informed just prior to the break that, again, as my colleague mentioned to you, because we speak the same language, we have to try to take it a bit slower, and especially to take some pauses between questions and answers. So I thought I was speaking slow, but we will try again to -- both to do our best to accommodate both the interpreters, but also the person taking down the transcript. So my next question concerns the material which was provided to you by the Prosecution. Now, the Defence has been provided with a list of all the documents which were given to you. And I guess you would agree with me, and you have already referred to the fact that it was quite substantial material.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I don't think you counted the number of pages, but if I say to you that -- if I suggest to you that there were a few thousands of pages, I think you would agree.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: You might be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you mentioned, you reviewed this material in order to produce your report, and in some cases, you actually read the material maybe two and sometimes three times. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: However, in drafting your report, you did not use all the documents which were given to you. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: You're correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in fact, according to what I have counted in your report, you used 104 documents out of more than 400. Is that a fair estimate?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Probably more than 400, but it might be right, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, am I right in saying that your opinion, even though you used only 104 documents, that your opinion is based on all the material which has been given to you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, because many documents are iterative in the content, saying similar things, and therefore, I thought I should not elaborate so much on the footnote. But you are right; this is a condensed version, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm sure that when you were looking at these documents, you had to assess the relevance of the documents, with a view to selecting the documents which would best illustrate your opinion. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, relevance is one thing, but I was wondering whether you verified the quality and the reliability of the documents you were provided with or whether you considered all material received to be facts you can use in drafting your report.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No. I tried to qualify them according to the questions and the case. And many documents, first of all, were not really related to what I was asked for -- to answer. And many documents were just pertaining to the individual criminal incidents on the spot, in which I did not interfere any much more, especially the witness statements, which had a huge amount of documents to be read.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Reinhardt, my question -- I'll try to be a bit more precise, in terms of: Did you assess the reliability of the document? For example, if a document did not bear a signature, is that something that you took into account?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, all the signatures, sir, which I saw were typed signatures. I never know whether these were official signatures or not. I tried to -- not I tried. I only used documents from which I thought that they were really giving some important information to that particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you receive any instructions or guidelines from the Prosecution as to whether some documents you should be careful in using them or some documents which were more reliable? Did you ever receive any instructions of that kind?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Negative, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you informed by the Prosecution, because you answered my last question in the negative, but were you informed by the Prosecution that the material you were provided with was not yet evidence in the trial?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I was only informed by the Prosecution that I should not base my statements on written witness statements, because written witness statements would not be as reliable as military documents. This was the only thing I ever heard in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you took this into consideration in drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we confirmed a little earlier that General Hadzihasanovic had already been indicted when you were approached by the Prosecution. Did they at any time inform you of what their views were towards the responsibility of the accused?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did they ever show you any documents with respect to their views in terms of: Did you ever see a document called a pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And moving on to witness statements, which my colleague referred to a little earlier on. Based on the lists of documents I was given, you were provided with 103 witness statements. Would that be more or less a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I think so, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you were not informed in terms of whether these witnesses had testified or would testify in the trial?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I give you two examples, and I use witness Blazevic Katica, a local witness, or witness Albert Hittmeyer, an international witness, statements of whom were provided to you, would I be right in saying that you were never informed that these people would not testify in the case?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, sir. I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in terms of the witness statements you were provided with, you don't know whether you had been provided with the witnesses who have or will testify?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No, sir. I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I give you two examples of witnesses the statements of whom you were not given, for example, Mr. Jeric, who was the military prosecutor in Travnik, and Mr. Kapetanovic, who was the senior public prosecutor in Zenica within the high prosecutor's office, would you be able to confirm that you were not given these statements?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if they are not on the list that I have, I guess that you were not given those statements.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would also like to refer to another example. There was a document which was given to you, and this document had the number 1474. I don't know if you have a list of your documents with you or if you could refer to this document referred to as PT174. It would be the testimony of a witness in the prior case, and the witness was called Major Dannatt.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: No. I haven't used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this witness statement was in fact given to you. Could you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this right now. Going through all those lists, because as long as I don't have the other numbers, they are in a different order. The order you just gave me, I really have to go page by page to re-find this. It would take a lot of time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So in order to save time, Mr. Reinhardt, I'd just like to show you the consolidated list of documents that we have been -- that we have received.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would like the usher, please, to show the witness simply that document, this document from Major Dannatt was actually given to you. [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't have copies for everybody. I just wanted the witness to confirm that he has indeed been provided with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] I have all the lists here, if you prefer to have all the lists, and we can of course show it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Okay. I see it right now. Unfortunately, I don't have the PT number listed down in the same order as you have it. Therefore it's very difficult for me to look back and forth. But it has been probably given to me, but I did not use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this document, Mr. Reinhardt, I would just like to, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, refer to a decision which dated on 23 January 2004. Sorry. [Interpretation] I'm going to continue in French, Mr. President. In this decision, the date is 23 January 2004, this document bears the number 115. That is the Prosecutor's list. And this is the document that is an excerpt from the testimony of the witness Major Dannatt in a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. previous case, in a prior case before this Tribunal. On the 23rd of January, 2004, the Trial Chamber decided that this document would not be admitted into evidence as a Prosecution exhibit. This is what I wanted to state for the record. This document was returned to the witness and, according to the decision of that Trial Chamber, it was not admitted among the exhibits that the witness had at his disposal. [In English] Mr. Reinhardt, on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has to reply. This document, 115, according to the Defence, has been returned to the witness. We need to know the date. The decision was rendered on the 23rd of January, 2004. Has the Prosecutor informed the witness that there's no date on this document? We have to verify. Maybe you'll be able to tell us more about it tomorrow, because at this moment I believe you cannot reply, I'm sure. Mr. Bourgon, can you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] I'm going to continue by going to the last draft of your report, or the second draft of your report, whereby the Trial Chamber issued a decision concerning some documents that were not to be used for the -- in terms of writing your report. One of these -- there were two documents. One related to each of the accused, which in fact was their prior testimony in a previous trial. Now, following this, you were asked by the Prosecution, in accordance with the instructions of the Trial Chamber, to submit a new report.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when I looked at the new report that you filed following these changes, I could not see any difference in your opinion with respect to the issue where you had used this document in your earlier draft. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have not changed the basic attitude of my statement because it was already confirmed based on the documents given to me before I have been issued this additional material by the Prosecutor, which I then incorporated. But while I incorporated it, it didn't change the basic statement which I had before. It only increased some of my findings, but it didn't change them. So I took all this out, but the basic outcome was not affected by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the same decision, the Trial Chamber requested that any opinion on the ultimate issue be removed, and I take it that you were informed by the Prosecution that this would be -- that that word was removed, and in fact you did remove it from your report. Now, my question to you is as follows: You did make a determination that you remove from the first report to the second report concerning the ultimate issue in this case?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in doing so, had you already decided in your mind on the criminal responsibility of the people against whom you are testifying today?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, I didn't decide on the criminal responsibility. I just laid down the case. And I was asked not to come up with any personal attitudes toward the accused and about their criminal responsibility or not. Therefore, I didn't go -- therefore, I didn't mention this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now, Mr. Reinhardt, to the third report that we were provided with. I guess it was two weeks ago. And I refer here to -- I guess it was given to us on the 22nd of April, 2004. And it includes a new report, the contents of which you are familiar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you explained earlier on, and I would like you to maybe elaborate a little more in terms of whether these changes were originated by you or whether they were originated by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Okay, sir. First of all, it's not a new report, because the text is with one little change absolutely the same. The question which -- or the things which are different are some of the footnotes, where I have different references to the footnote because I realised that in being mixed up with those four different ways of documenting the documents, or enumerating documents, I had made some mistakes. I did not been affected by anybody on that [sic]; just the contrary. First of all, I wrote an email to Mr. Withopf saying, "I made some mistakes here. Please -- I inform you that this has to be corrected." This was when I was halfway through. And when I went through with the rest of the things, checking every document again and again, against those four different ways of enumerating them, I found additional mistakes which I have made, and I told them there are additional mistakes. They have to be corrected. So this was my own realisation that I just did it not correctly in this regard, as far as the numbering of the footnote was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I would like to do is to go over a couple of these footnotes. Now, you would agree with me that footnotes in a report of this kind can be very important?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that because this document is indeed a document, like many others, which will be used to determine the liability of two people. So footnotes can be important.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to review a couple of these footnotes, starting with at footnote 5 of your report. Now, footnote 5 of your report was modified from the second to the third document, and footnote 5 is on page 3. Now, what was changed in footnote 5 is basically that you were referring to the regulations on the authority of a ground force corps commander in peacetime, and the number that was given was that of a telephone intercept which was a telephone intercept between Mr. Halilovic and someone called Dzedo on 16 June 1993. Now, this was modified to read and the text was changed to say these regulations prescribe the responsibilities of the land army corps command. Now, can you explain how a mistake like this could happen whereby you quote a document which happens to be the wrong document, and there's also a document in the numbering of the document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: I did not rewrite this footnote. I only changed the PT number from 1367, which I mistyped, in 1362.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So this would just a numbering mistake?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I move to footnote 9, which also appears to be a numbering mistake, where we have -- where you have written footnote -- or PT1221, and this was changed to PT474. Now, the first footnote you refer to the decree on -- the decree law on the army of BiH, whereas PT474 is the official army journal of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, what I'm curious about is that if you look in the report today, and if you look in paragraph 2.9, and I read on the fourth line. It says: "The rules of command authority are also laid down in the decree of the armed forces of BiH." Then we go to footnote 9, the new footnote approved by both yourself and the Prosecution is 474. Now, my problem is that 474 does not include -- is the wrong footnote.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Sir, in my final report, which I issued, it's still 1221, and this is the decree with the powers of law of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm sorry. This is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We were given a document here in which footnote 12 -- footnote 9 was changed from PT1221 to PT474.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, but I haven't changed this. There must be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I mean -- by all means, if you think it's a mistake, I take your word, and I'm not here to -- I hope you understand that this procedure is to solidify, to make sure that we have a firm base from which to work on in the morning.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the PT1221, which is quoted into your report.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: The decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And PT1221 is the decree of the armed forces of BiH. And if I look at 1221, it's called decree law on the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if this was changed, this was then changed -- or it was a mistake changed by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Well, the 1221, sir, is the decree with the powers of law of the armed forces, which is the one which I quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I move on to footnote 50 -- sorry. Footnote 22. Sorry, I skipped a page. Footnote 22. And this is in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Reinhardt. I just had a quick question from my colleague, and indeed you did have the right footnote before this change was made in terms of the fact that this footnote, the footnote 9, was 1221 and should have remained 1221. So I don't know what could have happened. So in footnote 22, it was indicated PT471, and it was changed to PT1144. Would that be a wrong number or would that be something else?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: The number 471 basically is an overall presidential order which has the decree law on military courts. It's the basic order which established this. And 1144 is then the decree law on special military courts. So what I want you to note here, and therefore I want to have this amended it is 471 plus 1144. Because the real contents of the law is in 1144.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it's plus. So --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: It's a plus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With a plus?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. And I move on to footnote 29. I don't have too many footnotes. Just the footnotes that were referred to us by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- the changes. And I have four or five, I guess, so it shouldn't take too long. In footnote 29, there was a reference to a PT -- sorry. It's footnote 29, yes. There was a PT478.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my problem with this particular document is that you were only provided, at least according to our documents, with a very short summary --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- which does not talk about the fact that the commander was entrusted with the building of the corps. So I'm just curious, because if I look at your footnote 29, in the text, and it reads here: "As the first commander of the 3rd Corps, Enver Hadzihasanovic was made responsible for its organisation and build-up." And footnote 29 says PT478. Now, I can give you PT478, and at least in my reading of the document, it doesn't refer to the fact that Enver Hadzihasanovic was made responsible for the build-up of the corps.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: If I read the summary, the first sentence, it says: "According to the security administration information, Enver Hadzihasanovic plus Morad Mikivic [phoen] are engaged in organisation of the 3rd Corps in Zenica." And this is clear to me, that he is responsible for building up the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The fact that he's engaged in the organisation of the corps. I mean, I take your assessment of these words, but that is your reading of those words --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- is that he was made responsible for the build-up of the corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to the footnote 78. But before that, this refers to, of course, paragraph 4.22 in your report. Now, in paragraph 4.22 of your report, there was a modification that was made, where the first thing is, and I read towards the end of the paragraph, the fourth line to the end, where it says: "According to the legal obligations of Article 239 of the RBiH criminal law," and that was crossed out and replaced with: "regulations of international laws of war in the armed forces of the SFRY." Is that a change that you triggered, or whose decision is it to say that Article 239 does not apply than it should be the regulations of the international laws of war?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: This was a mistake which I found out, which I haven't corrected, and therefore, I asked last time that we correct this. This was my finding out to the mistake here. I misquoted from the wrong document. 239, Article 239 has a total different meaning of that particular criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this PT1222, you asked for this to be replaced, and I take it that the Prosecution did not discuss with you and they replaced it as you had requested?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: They have -- they rewrote it -- I rewrote it and gave it to them and asked them to replace it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, of course, my colleague referred to the fact that you are not a lawyer. But I think you know that for a law to apply to somebody, the law has to be in force. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, from the documents that you've read, I take it that you know that when the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina became an independent state, they actually enacted a number of laws from their former country which became law in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you actually quote an example of this in -- which is included in PT3, basically where it is a known fact that the Criminal Code of the SFRY became law in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what would you say if I suggest to you that in terms of these regulations on the international laws of war in the armed forces of the SFRY, this law was not enacted as law in Bosnia? What would your reaction be?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Then my assumption was wrong. My assumption was that this was also a part of these regulations and laws applicable now to the new Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this specific paragraph, because this is one of the foundations of your report, whereas you say that the commander was responsible for everything that happened in his specific area of responsibility. So you basically say there's an area and everything that happens in the area, the commander was responsible. Now, I would agree with you that this regulation of the SFRY somehow referred to that, but if it is not in force, did you find any laws or any regulations in force in Bosnia that said that the commander was responsible for everything that happened in his area?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: This was the main quotation. I didn't find any other. This is the key document for that. And therefore, I was -- sir, therefore, I was keen to have it changed, because I realised I made a mistake here. And this was one of the key questions I wanted to come back here and say: There is a question. I have to have it changed because I quoted on the wrong -- on the wrong foot here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to footnote 115. And I cut short because we were advised to stop at 10 to 7.00. So I'll just maybe do this 115 and tomorrow I'll have just two or three and then we can move on to really the substance of the report. But in footnote 115, there was a new PT which was added. Now, I quote from paragraph 8.2, and it says, the third line from the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bottom: "They reacted by repeatedly addressing such actions and behaviour and by giving written orders to stop them immediately. The first documents to this effect occurred in February of 1993 and continued to appear throughout the year." Now, this is footnote 115 and footnote 116. And a new PT39 was added.
