Was this at your request? And if so, why? Because you had already given examples. Or was it because you were invited to do so?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Sir, 215, the third one in 155. In my translation to my files with A, B, C, and in these A, B, C, different numbers, I just called the wrong thing, and therefore, I had to replace it. 215 was the wrong document, and I replaced it with the right document, which is 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But according to my information, 215 was not replaced; just 39 was added. That's what I have from the information --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- that was provided to me by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT
utterances.text: 215 has nothing to do with what I'm expressing here. It has to be deleted. It has to be replaced by 39. I basically had the mistake in the translation of the documents and I pulled the wrong document. And when I realised this, I put in the document I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you very much for your answers, Mr. Reinhardt. I guess we have to stop for today. Tomorrow I have two or three documents like that I would like to get further explanation and then we move on to the substance. Because we are very interested in getting -- as I've mentioned before, to benefiting from your military knowledge. And I hope you understand that this is meant to establish, affirm documents from which we can work. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that concludes the cross-examination for today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Before we started hearing the witness, we discussed the matter of the duration of the cross-examination. You said that it would take you 12 hours, Mr. Bourgon, to cross-examine the witness, and Mr. Kubura's Defence counsel informed us that they would need 2 hours, and you said that the Judges could use the remaining time. According to your calculations, we should have hearings that last about 20 hours. We have made our own calculations and we -- the result we obtained wasn't the same as yours. If starting from Today, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, we have 3 hours and 45 minutes if we subtract the breaks. We start at 9.00 and adjourn at 1345, so in fact we have 3 hours and 45 minutes each day. When we multiply 3.45 by 4, we obtain a total of 15 hours. So tomorrow we'll have another 15 hours at our disposal. You will need 10 hours out of these 15, because you have already cross-examined the witness for two hours. Mr. Dixon or Ibrisimovic will need two hours. So the Judges will only have about three hours, if we -- and we also have to include the Prosecution's additional questions. Mr. Bourgon, weren't you a little too optimistic when you made your calculations? When you said you would need 12 hours, is there a possibility of reducing the time you need? Unless you think that you could also cross-examine next week, but that would make it necessary for the witness to be available next week too, on Monday and on Tuesday. I will first ask the witness before I let you take the floor. General Reinhardt, you've been scheduled to testify during this week. Would it be possible for you to continue giving testimony next week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, we must conclude with hearing this witness on Friday. Mr. Bourgon, according to our calculations, we can't follow the timetable, because the Prosecution and the Judges won't even have three hours to cross-examine the witness, because you will have taken up almost all the time. My other question is: You have 12 hours and Mr. Kubura's Defence will be taking 2 hours. You will need six times more time, whereas in fact the questions might be quite the same. Well, what can you tell us about this? I must point out that given the witness's obligations, we have to conclude on Friday at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have discussed this matter with the Prosecution, and we would like to conclude on Friday, as planned. So we will do all we can to make this possible. When I calculated the hours, I was basing myself on four hours a day. But my intention, Mr. President, was to conclude halfway through Thursday. So I'll cross-examine for four hours tomorrow, four hours the day after tomorrow, and two hours on Thursday morning, and then Mr. Kubura's Defence can conclude. Without counting the exact number of hours needed, I think, Mr. President, that it would be possible for the Defence to conclude its cross-examination at the end of Thursday, and that would mean that the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution would have Friday to ask their questions. We'll do what we can to reduce the time we need, but there are a number of documents that we would like to discuss with the witness. At the moment, we're trying to find a way of proceeding more effectively, a way of avoiding any loss of time when referring to documents. We'll try to conclude at the end of Thursday. And if we use up more time, perhaps we could continue to work a little longer on Friday, if any problems do arise. But, Mr. President, if the Trial Chamber accepts the suggestion, I think that we could conclude at the end of Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the documents are concerned, the ones you have mentioned, how many of them are there? And in your opinion, the documents you will be presenting, are they documents that might result in the Prosecution asking additional questions? And will any new issues be raised when dealing with these document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As far as admissibility is concerned, if there are any new documents - and in fact, there are some new documents - if our colleagues from the Prosecution agree - naturally, we haven't discussed this matter yet - we intend to have them all marked for identification. As a result, we won't have to discuss the question of admissibility and we can take full use of the presence of the expert witness. As far as the question as to whether the documents will give rise to any new issues, we do not believe that any new issues will be raised. We believe that the Prosecution will be aware of the purpose for which we are cross-examining the witness with regard to these documents. But certain issues might be raised on the basis of the these documents. This is not a possibility I can exclude. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, in the light of what has been said, what would your comment be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll limit my comments, due to the time. Certainly, in the absence of any indication as to which documents Mr. Bourgon is referring to, where they came from, we're really not in a position to fully explain whether or not it might give rise to new issues. We don't have any of the documents he's referring to. We don't know if they're documents that we disclosed to the Defence, if they're documents that the Defence investigators turned up on their own. We simply don't know how many documents, what the documents refer to, et cetera. So it's certainly not possible for us to give a final determination as to whether those documents would result in the need for re-examination or not. We're certainly open to the idea of marking the documents in advance to expedite the proceedings, and of course any advance notice that we have or any advance disclosure of the documents to the Prosecution would allow us to be in a better position to make a determination as to whether re-examination is required in light of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In view of what both parties have said, the Trial Chamber notes that the Defence will attempt to conclude its cross-examination by 1.45 on Thursday. We will then have Friday morning for the Judges' questions and, similarly, for the Prosecution to re-examine the witness. We'll see the matter more clearly on the basis of the documents that you have to present. As far as the excerpt of the decision is concerned, what did you want to do with it? Did you want to request that it be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since I read this decision out loud and it's been included in the transcript, I don't think it's necessary to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. It's 7.00 p.m. exactly now. General, we will now adjourn and we will resume tomorrow at 9.00. Given that you have made the solemn declaration, you're in the hands of justice now. Naturally, you shouldn't have any form of contact with either of the parties. So please appear tomorrow for the hearing that will start at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
